stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin Hold Their First Three-Way Meeting in Shenzhen; Joint Statement Leaves Out Ukraine
stories.what_happened: On Thursday 19 November, US President Donald Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin held their first-ever three-way meeting, at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. It lasted about an hour and a half and ended with a short joint statement on UN reform, more oil and gas production, limits on the International Criminal Court and avoiding nuclear war. The statement did not mention Ukraine, and Putin ruled out talks with Ukraine for now.
stories.why_it_matters: The three leaders run three of the world's most powerful countries, all permanent members of the UN Security Council; but neither Ukraine nor European governments were in the room, and the meeting brought no breakthrough on the war.

key_facts.fact: Trump, Xi and Putin held their first-ever trilateral meeting on Thursday 19 November at Kylin Villa, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.
The three-way meeting lasted roughly an hour and a half.
Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then with Xi.
The Kremlin released a joint statement, and the White House later provided the same text.
In the joint statement the three leaders, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reaffirmed a commitment to reforming the United Nations.
The joint statement committed to increasing gas and oil production 'for the benefit of all countries'.
The joint statement said the International Criminal Court and similar bodies should not abuse their powers.
The joint statement said 'there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed.'
The three leaders' joint declaration made no mention of the war in Ukraine or any new peace initiative.
Putin ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine after a Ukrainian strike on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea, saying: 'We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge.'
Putin said Ukraine and Europe were 'not yet ready' to compromise.
Putin said all three leaders agreed it was a 'useful format' and that such meetings could happen again.
Putin said he would consider attending the G20 summit in Miami in December after discussing it with Trump.
Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of 0 to 10, and said of Putin when shaking his hand: 'He's my friend.'
Trump said he spoke with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, mainly about trade and tariffs; Xi said relations were 'stable and improved'.
A US-China tariff truce expires on 10 January next year; tariffs went above 100% during the 2025 trade war.
Trump said he would ask China to 'do some more' for American farmers.
Trump told Fox News that he and Xi share an interest in safety-focused rules for artificial intelligence and plan to cooperate on them.
Neither Ukraine's government nor European officials were in the room.
Before the summit, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called it a 'huge mistake' for major powers to make decisions about smaller nations without their involvement.
In Berlin, Zelensky avoided questions about the Shenzhen meeting, saying Putin probably raised certain issues with Trump but that they do not know what was discussed.
Ukraine's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said no decisions can be made without Ukraine.
The war in Ukraine is in its fifth year, more than four years after Russia's invasion.
China is a major buyer of Iranian oil and Russia has ties to Iran.
Analyst Andrius Tursa of Teneo called the summit 'arguably a diplomatic victory for Moscow'.
The Kremlin said it would continue dialogue with China and the US on reducing nuclear risks.
Trump said he would hold a news briefing at noon on Friday after returning from the trip.
Putin walked over to Trump at the group photo and shook his hand while Xi looked on; it was their first meeting since their Alaska summit in August 2025.

stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan Crosses the South Odisha Coast Near Gopalpur, Weaker and Farther North Than Forecast; 3.72 Lakh People Evacuated
stories.what_happened: Cyclone Akvan crossed the south Odisha coast near Gopalpur on the morning of Friday 20 November. It had weakened from a severe cyclonic storm to a cyclonic storm before landfall, and came ashore farther north than first forecast, then weakened into a deep depression. Odisha moved about 3.72 lakh people to nearly 10,000 shelters, and officials reported no casualties or major damage so far.
stories.why_it_matters: Early warnings and large evacuations are how India keeps people safe from cyclones; heavy rain and flood alerts continue in Odisha and north Andhra Pradesh.

key_facts.fact: Cyclonic storm Akvan crossed the south Odisha coast near Gopalpur on Friday 20 November.
The IMD said the cyclone crossed the coast between 7.30 and 8.30 am, with winds of 70-80 kmph gusting up to 90 kmph.
Akvan was a severe cyclonic storm until Thursday night and weakened into a cyclonic storm by Friday morning.
The storm had earlier been expected to cross mid-coastal Andhra Pradesh but changed course and moved toward north Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

Earlier IMD guidance placed landfall between Nellore and Visakhapatnam around midday as a very severe cyclonic storm; Akvan instead crossed farther north near Gopalpur, several hours earlier and at a lower intensity.
IMD Director General Mrutyunjay Mohapatra had said: 'The centre of the cyclone, known as the eye in meteorological terms, will cross the coast near Gopalpur in Odisha.'
After landfall the system moved north-northeastward through Odisha and weakened into a deep depression; by 14:30 IST it was about 80 km north of Gopalpur.
About 3.72 lakh people were evacuated from vulnerable areas and moved to nearly 10,000 shelters in Odisha.
Odisha Chief Secretary Anu Garg said there were 'no reports of casualties or major damage received so far.'
4,470 pregnant women were moved to safety; 1,450 of them have given birth, and mothers and newborns are safe.
In the 24 hours to 8:30 am on Friday, the IMD station at Gopalpur recorded 180.4 mm of rain, and Ganjam district averaged 114.06 mm, the highest of any district.
A red alert for extremely heavy rain was issued for Balasore and Mayurbhanj in Odisha.
The IMD issued a red alert for extremely heavy rain for Srikakulam and Vizianagaram districts of Andhra Pradesh.
A storm surge of 0.5 to 1 metre above the astronomical tide could flood low-lying coastal areas of Ganjam and Puri around landfall.
Gopalpur port hoisted Great Danger Signal 10, and Paradip port Great Danger Signal 9.
South Eastern Railway cancelled at least 28 express trains for Friday, most going to or through Puri, including the Howrah-Puri Vande Bharat Express.
East Coast Railway cancelled around 45 trains and rescheduled around 28 over three days.
Waterlogging was reported on roads in Berhampur and Digapahandi, and teams were sent to clear rainwater.
Authorities deployed 423 rescue teams.

stories.headline: COP31 Heads Into Overtime After a New Draft Drops Any Mention of Fossil Fuels
stories.what_happened: At the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, a revised nine-page draft agreement published on 19 November contains no explicit reference to fossil fuels and drops a proposed $120 billion-a-year target for adaptation money. Panama threatened to formally object, campaigners called it a backward step, and negotiators expected the talks, due to end on Friday 20 November, to run into Saturday.
stories.why_it_matters: COP agreements guide how almost 200 countries tackle climate change; the draft would be the first COP text to recognise the world will not meet the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree goal.

key_facts.fact: COP31 is being held in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators from almost 200 countries.
The conference began on 9 November and was scheduled to end on Friday 20 November.
The revised draft is nine pages long, down from 18 pages in Monday's draft, and contains 'no explicit reference to fossil fuels'.
The first draft's call to speed up the COP28 commitment to move away from coal, oil and gas has been dropped.
The draft drops a proposed target of at least $120 billion a year by 2035 for developing countries' adaptation funding; the COP30 commitment to triple adaptation money remains.
The draft keeps a goal to raise electricity's share of total global energy use from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035, but does not say it must come from renewables like solar and wind.
Australia's Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations, said COP31 would be the first summit to recognise the world will not meet the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree ambition.
COP31 President Murat Kurum said the electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels.
Panama vowed to 'formally object' if the final agreement doesn't add climate finance, cap oil production and acknowledge failing goals.
Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa called the revision a 'backward step'.
In 2023, at COP28 in Dubai, countries called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time.
Negotiators worked through Thursday night into Friday and expected COP31 to run into overtime on Saturday.
The agreements are adopted by nearly 200 nations and are voluntary and non-binding.
Host Turkey says it agreed deals and plans worth more than $26 billion during the summit, including a preliminary $15 billion renewable energy deal with China.
The next climate summit is scheduled for November 2027 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
The EU is assessing the draft; European Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra set three tests for it, including whether it responds adequately to the climate crisis.

stories.headline: Atmospheric river storm floods California streets and buries the Sierra in snow
stories.what_happened: A powerful atmospheric river storm swept across California on 18-19 November 2026, breaking a 108-year-old daily rain record in San Francisco and triggering water rescues and mudslides around Los Angeles. Heavy snow closed mountain passes in the Sierra Nevada.
stories.why_it_matters: Atmospheric rivers bring much of California's water, but too much rain at once causes floods, especially on land burned by wildfires; forecasters link this wet season to a strong El Niño.

key_facts.fact: An atmospheric river is a long, narrow plume of moisture that can flow thousands of miles high in the atmosphere, like a fire hose in the sky; storms release it as heavy rain and mountain snow.
On Wednesday 18 November downtown San Francisco set a daily rainfall record of 2.28 inches, beating the 2.24-inch record set in 1918.
On Thursday 19 November the Los Angeles area got more than 3 inches of rain in 12 hours; helicopters lifted one person out of a flood control channel and crews pulled a woman from a submerged car.
Mudslides were reported across the San Fernando Valley, and LA County and Malibu issued evacuation warnings for areas burned by recent wildfires.
Burned ground cannot absorb as much water, so heavy rain can loosen soil and send it washing downhill as debris flows.
More than 200 flights at Los Angeles International Airport were delayed on Thursday, about 12% of traffic.
Rock and mud slides in Big Sur closed more than 40 miles of Highway 1.
Winter storm warnings called for 1 to 3 feet of snow above 4,000 feet and over 5 feet on the highest Sierra peaks; mountain passes closed.
A potentially historic super El Niño is boosting California's odds of a wet winter, with more atmospheric river storms likely in coming weeks and months.

stories.headline: Senate narrowly rejects resolution to pull US forces out of the Iran war
stories.what_happened: On 19 November 2026 the Senate voted 48-51 against a resolution, already passed by the House in September, that would have directed the president to remove US armed forces from hostilities with Iran. It was Congress's first vote on the war since the 3 November midterm elections.
stories.why_it_matters: The US Constitution splits power over war between Congress and the president, and this vote shows lawmakers testing that balance; it also shows how one or two senators changing sides can decide a close vote.

key_facts.fact: The Senate rejected the Iran war powers resolution 48-51 on Thursday, 19 November 2026; the House had adopted it in mid-September.
The resolution would have directed the president 'to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.'
Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul voted for it; Democrat John Fetterman voted against it.
Republican Thom Tillis, who had backed an earlier effort, voted against, saying 'this one doesn't go to the president, so it's just a statement from Congress.'
Because it was a concurrent resolution, it would not have gone to the president for signature, so even if passed it would have been largely symbolic.
Democrat Tim Kaine said the war's unpopularity 'was made absolutely manifestly clear in the election results from Nov. 3.'
As of 13 November the war had cost at least $48.3 billion, not counting damage to US bases.
Under the Constitution, authority over the use of the military is divided between Congress and the President.

Congress passed the War Powers Resolution on 7 November 1973 over President Nixon's veto; it requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of sending forces into hostilities and to end their use after 60 days unless Congress authorises it.

Congress must pass a government funding bill to avoid a shutdown after 11 December, and some Democrats are debating whether to cut off war funding there or wait until they control Congress in January.
Rep. Thomas Massie plans to force another House war powers vote before the lame-duck session ends.
Since the war with Iran began in late February, Democrats have forced more than a dozen war powers votes in Congress, and most have failed.

stories.headline: Senate passes bipartisan bill to speed up approval of energy projects; House votes next
stories.what_happened: On 19 November 2026 the US Senate voted 62-33 to pass a big bipartisan 'permitting' bill that changes how the government reviews and approves power lines, wind and solar farms, mines and oil drilling. It now goes to the House of Representatives, which is expected to take it up after the Thanksgiving holiday; if both chambers pass it, the president must sign it to make it law.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how a US bill becomes law (both houses, then the president) and how lawmakers from rival parties sometimes trade wins to get a deal; supporters say it will speed up building energy projects, while environmental groups warn it weakens nature protections.

key_facts.fact: The Senate passed the permitting bill 62-33 on Thursday, 19 November 2026.
The official Senate roll call lists 62 yeas, 33 nays and 5 senators not voting; a simple majority (1/2) was required.

The bill is called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act; 15 Democrats joined nearly all Republicans in support, and Republicans Mike Rounds and Josh Hawley were the only Republicans to oppose it.
It was led by four senators from both parties: Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.).

It changes how reviews are done and permits issued under laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act and the Clean Water Act, covering power lines, wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling.
NEPA is a bedrock environmental law that requires federal agencies to weigh a project's likely environmental effects before approving it; the bill limits legal challenges under NEPA.

The bill gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines and includes provisions meant to stop ordinary electricity customers paying the power costs of data centres.

Supporters included the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association and the US Chamber of Commerce, and the White House backed it; opponents included the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, 17 Democratic-led states and the National Congress of American Indians.
Capito said the bill 'threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while.'

The bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess; Speaker Mike Johnson said it can pass, but many Democrats want to wait until the new Congress in January, when their party will have larger majorities.
Earlier efforts failed: a 2022 attempt by Sen. Joe Manchin lost a 47-47 procedural vote, and a 2024 bill never got a full Senate vote.

stories.headline: Record November rains flood Florida's Space Coast; St. Johns River tops 1953 record
stories.what_happened: Days of torrential rain that hit South Florida moved north to the Space Coast on 19 November 2026, overflowing rivers and leading to nearly 100 high-water rescues in Brevard County, including dozens of horses. The St. Johns River near Cocoa rose above its 1953 record flood level.
stories.why_it_matters: November is normally part of Florida's dry season; the record rain shows how El Niño can reshape weather on both US coasts at once.

key_facts.fact: Fort Lauderdale-area rain totals were nearly 17 inches over 48 hours, according to preliminary National Weather Service figures.
Fort Lauderdale, Melbourne and West Palm Beach recorded their wettest November on record.
Parts of Brevard County got about 40 inches of rain in three weeks, roughly 70% of their normal yearly rainfall.
Sheriff Wayne Ivey said first responders had made nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county; volunteers saved 40 animals in 30 minutes at an equestrian centre in Cocoa.
The St. Johns River near Cocoa rose above its 1953 record flood level.
Nearly 200 Florida National Guard members and 50 high-water vehicles were deployed; about 5 million people were under a flood watch on 20 November.
Florida's dry season normally runs from October to May, and El Niño conditions are expected to last through spring.

stories.headline: NASA pauses Perseverance rover's science while fixing radio problems; Mars Odyssey also troubled
stories.what_happened: NASA said on 19 November 2026 that its Perseverance rover on Mars has paused science work while engineers investigate problems with both of its UHF radios. Separately, the 25-year-old Mars Odyssey orbiter, which relays data from Mars rovers, lost a spinning wheel it uses to point itself.
stories.why_it_matters: Robots on Mars depend on radios and relay satellites to talk to Earth; the story shows how engineers build in backups and fix spacecraft millions of kilometres away.

key_facts.fact: On 30 October Perseverance's primary radio stopped sending its regular 'heartbeat' signal; after 25 missed heartbeats (about 100 seconds) the rover switched to its backup radio and went into safe mode.
Engineers then found the backup radio was transmitting at about half its expected power, so both radios are out of use for now.
The rover is stable and talking directly to NASA's Deep Space Network over a much slower link, so science is paused to save bandwidth; NASA hopes to resume science by the end of November.
Mars Odyssey had a reaction wheel stop spinning; it needs at least three wheels to orient itself, and one of its original four already failed in 2013.
Without the wheels Odyssey must use hydrazine thrusters, and estimates show enough fuel for that for roughly one to two months.
Odyssey launched in April 2001, was designed to last just over 2.5 years, and has orbited Mars for about 25 years, longer than any other Mars mission.

stories.headline: Justice Department moves to end its lawsuit over Alaska's Senate election after Peltola wins
stories.what_happened: On 19 November 2026 the US Justice Department asked a federal appeals court to declare its lawsuit over Alaska's Senate race 'moot' (no longer needed), because Democrat Mary Peltola won the election outright. The suit had tried to block the state from certifying the result if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lost.
stories.why_it_matters: In the US, states run elections and certify (officially confirm) the results; this case shows how courts handle challenges to that process and why ballot secrecy matters.

key_facts.fact: The Justice Department asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday to declare its lawsuit moot, citing Peltola's victory.
The suit, filed in October, sought to block certification unless Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan won; it centred on a second candidate on the ballot with a similar name, independent Dan J. Sullivan.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the case on 1 November, two days before the election, finding prosecutors lacked standing.
Peltola won with more than 50% of first-choice votes, so Alaska's ranked-choice counting rounds were not needed and votes for either Sullivan did not change the result.

Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward wrote that the government 'reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means' of telling whether votes for Dan J. Sullivan were meant for the incumbent.
Peltola's victory was confirmed on 17 November and Alaska plans to certify it on 25 November.
The League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause asked the appeals court to uphold the dismissal and consider sanctions against federal lawyers.

stories.headline: India and Japan agree closer defence and supply-chain ties at Tokyo '2+2' talks
stories.what_happened: India's foreign minister S. Jaishankar and defence minister Rajnath Singh met Japan's foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi and defence minister Shinjiro Koizumi in Tokyo on 19 November for the fourth India-Japan '2+2' dialogue. They agreed to work together on defence technology, sea security and supply chains for things like computer chips and critical minerals, and India will let Japanese forces train with missiles on Indian firing ranges.
stories.why_it_matters: A '2+2' meeting puts both countries' foreign and defence ministers in one room, which shows how close a partnership is. The two countries are trying to make sure no single country can cut off the supplies their economies depend on.

key_facts.fact: The fourth India-Japan 2+2 ministerial dialogue was held in Tokyo on Thursday 19 November 2026, with S. Jaishankar and Rajnath Singh for India and Toshimitsu Motegi and Shinjiro Koizumi for Japan.
The four ministers met for 90 minutes.

Under a letter of intent, Indian firing ranges will be opened to live-fire training by Japan's Self-Defense Forces, including surface-to-ship missiles; IntelliNews reported Japanese forces will fire missiles on Indian ranges for the first time.

The sides agreed to build resilient supply chains through project-based cooperation in semiconductors, critical minerals, clean energy, information and communication technology (ICT) and pharmaceuticals.

The joint statement expressed 'grave concern' over 'economic coercion' and 'arbitrary export restrictions' without naming any country; Jaishankar spoke of a 'growing tendency to weaponise connectivity, resources, services, supply chains and market shares'.

The UNICORN project, Japanese-designed integrated antenna masts for Indian Navy warships, was described as the first defence equipment transfer project between the two countries; Tokyo expects India to grant Acceptance of Necessity by February 2027 under a 'Design with Japan, Make in India' label.
India's DRDO and Japan's defence technology agency ATLA will begin joint research on missiles and other advanced defence technology.
Each country supports the other's bid for a permanent seat on a reformed UN Security Council.
They agreed to work on secure undersea cable networks in the Indo-Pacific, AI-enabled cybersecurity and space situational awareness.
The ministers condemned terrorism in all its forms, including cross-border terrorism, and named UN-listed groups including Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammad.
India-Japan trade was about $27.5 billion in fiscal 2025-26, and Tokyo has pledged to invest JPY 10 trillion (about $62.5 billion) in India over a decade.
The next 2+2 meeting will be held in India at a mutually convenient date; the two countries mark 75 years of diplomatic relations in 2027.
The previous (third) 2+2 round was held in New Delhi on 20 August 2024.

stories.headline: Modi opens first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum at Delhi's Purana Qila
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Narendra Modi opened the first Civilisational Dialogue Forum of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) at Purana Qila, a 16th-century fort in New Delhi, on 20 November. Delegates from SCO countries, including Pakistan's minister Musadik Malik, are attending talks, exhibitions and shows about shared history, art, music, food and languages.
stories.why_it_matters: The SCO usually talks about security and trade; this forum is about culture, and Modi argued that knowing each other's history and arts helps keep peace between countries.

stories.headline: Senate narrowly rejects resolution to pull US forces out of the Iran war
stories.what_happened: On 19 November 2026 the Senate voted 48-51 against a resolution, already passed by the House in September, that would have directed the president to remove US armed forces from hostilities with Iran. stories.why_it_matters: The US Constitution splits power over war between Congress and the president, and this vote shows lawmakers testing that balance; it also shows how one or two senators changing sides can decide a close vote.

key_facts.fact: The Senate rejected the Iran war powers resolution 48-51 on Thursday, 19 November 2026; the House had adopted it in mid-September.
The resolution would have directed the president 'to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.'
Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul voted for it; Democrat John Fetterman voted against it.
Republican Thom Tillis, who had backed an earlier effort, voted against, saying 'this one doesn't go to the president, so it's just a statement from Congress.'
Because it was a concurrent resolution, it would not have gone to the president for signature, so even if passed it would have been largely symbolic.
Democrat Tim Kaine said the war's unpopularity 'was made absolutely manifestly clear in the election results from Nov. 3.'
As of 13 November the war had cost at least $48.3 billion, not counting damage to US bases.
Under the Constitution, authority over the use of the military is divided between Congress and the President.

Congress passed the War Powers Resolution on 7 November 1973 over President Nixon's veto; it requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of sending forces into hostilities and to end their use after 60 days unless Congress authorises it.

Congress must pass a government funding bill to avoid a shutdown after 11 December, and some Democrats are debating whether to cut off war funding there or wait until they control Congress in January.

stories.headline: Senate passes bipartisan bill to speed up approval of energy projects; House votes next
stories.what_happened: On 19 November 2026 the US Senate voted 62-33 to pass a big bipartisan 'permitting' bill that changes how the government reviews and approves power lines, wind and solar farms, mines and oil drilling. It now goes to the House of Representatives, which is expected to take it up after the Thanksgiving holiday; if both chambers pass it, the president must sign it to make it law.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how a US bill becomes law (both houses, then the president) and how lawmakers from rival parties sometimes trade wins to get a deal; supporters say it will speed up building energy projects, while environmental groups warn it weakens nature protections.

key_facts.fact: The Senate passed the permitting bill 62-33 on Thursday, 19 November 2026.
The official Senate roll call lists 62 yeas, 33 nays and 5 senators not voting; a simple majority (1/2) was required.

The bill is called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act; 15 Democrats joined nearly all Republicans in support, and Republicans Mike Rounds and Josh Hawley were the only Republicans to oppose it.
It was led by four senators from both parties: Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.).

It changes how reviews are done and permits issued under laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act and the Clean Water Act, covering power lines, wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling.
NEPA is a bedrock environmental law that requires federal agencies to weigh a project's likely environmental effects before approving it; the bill limits legal challenges under NEPA.

The bill gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines and includes provisions meant to stop ordinary electricity customers paying the power costs of data centres.

Supporters included the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association and the US Chamber of Commerce, and the White House backed it; opponents included the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, 17 Democratic-led states and the National Congress of American Indians.
Capito said the bill 'threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while.'

The bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess; Speaker Mike Johnson said it can pass, but many Democrats want to wait until the new Congress in January, when their party will have larger majorities.

stories.headline: Brain area known for listening also plans our words before we speak, study finds
stories.what_happened: A study published in the journal Science on 19 November 2026 found that a small part of Wernicke's area, a brain region long thought to be mainly for understanding speech, also prepares whole words about a quarter of a second before a person says them. Researchers led by Edward Chang recorded brain activity from 28 people who were having surgery for epilepsy or tumours.
stories.why_it_matters: It challenges a view of the brain that is about 150 years old, and could help surgeons protect speech during operations and help build brain implants that let people who cannot speak communicate.

key_facts.fact: The study was published in Science on 19 November 2026 (DOI 10.1126/science.aef8963).
Researchers recorded brain activity from 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumours.
The area studied is the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), a small part of Wernicke's area; it became active both when people listened to words and just before they tried to speak.
Edward Chang said a word 'began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it'.

How it works: the neurons encode complete, specific words rather than basic sounds, including features such as word length, number of syllables and how often a word is used; neurons controlling the mouth then turn this plan into speech movements.
Some cells preferred long words: Matthew Leonard said the area is more active before 'caterpillar' than before 'cat'.
Electrical stimulation of the lpSTG just before speaking disrupted speech, and lesions in the area disrupted the ability to produce speech.
Carl Wernicke first described the area in 1874 as necessary for understanding speech.
Deep-learning models decoded intended speech from two people with paralysis who silently attempted to say a set of words.
Outside expert Jeffrey Binder said: 'My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area'.
The authors suggest Wernicke's area could become a target for future speech neuroprostheses (brain implants that restore speech); the area's exact boundaries remain uncertain.

stories.headline: Astronomers watch a giant star in Andromeda swallow its smaller partner
stories.what_happened: A study published in Nature on 18 November 2026 reconstructed how a small star spiralled into a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away. The giant brightened for seven years and then erupted in October 2025; the event, officially AT 2025abao, was nicknamed 'Bao'. Telescopes including NASA's James Webb Space Telescope tracked it.
stories.why_it_matters: Lead author Viraj Karambelkar said the event provides the first observations of a long-predicted process, in which a star is swallowed by its partner, helping scientists understand how pairs of stars live and die.

key_facts.fact: The study was published in Nature on 18 November 2026; lead author is Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University.
The giant star is about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy.
The giant is about seven times the Sun's mass and 350 times its width; the companion was about 70% of the Sun's mass.
For seven years, beginning in 2018, the giant grew brighter and swelled to more than twice its original size, then erupted in October 2025.

How it works: the smaller star ('Little Bao') orbited inside the giant's ('Big Bao') outer gas layers; the gas pushed back, creating drag that made it spiral inward and hand energy to the gas, some of which escaped as light, making the giant shine brighter. Astronomers call this 'common-envelope evolution'.
The team estimates only about a tenth of the giant's outer gas escaped in the eruption, and the energy of the fast-moving gas suggests the small star reached the giant's core.
Many telescopes contributed: NEOWISE first flagged a change in February 2023, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption on 17 October 2025, and Webb observed the system on 24 December 2025.
Karambelkar said: 'I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this' and 'Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult.'
It is not yet certain: Karambelkar notes both stars might instead have survived in a much tighter orbit, and dust blocks a direct view of what remains.
The system will take years or decades to settle; the researchers plan to search for similar systems and hope to catch them before they erupt.

stories.headline: Europe picks seven-spacecraft mission to study how the Sun's energy hits Earth's magnetic shield
stories.what_happened: On 19 November 2026 the European Space Agency's Science Programme Committee selected Plasma Observatory as its next medium-class science mission. Seven spacecraft will fly together and measure magnetic fields, electric fields and particles at seven places at once. Launch is provisionally foreseen for the late 2030s.
stories.why_it_matters: The solar wind's clash with Earth's magnetic field causes auroras and, at its most extreme, can knock out satellites and power grids, so understanding it matters for space weather.

key_facts.fact: ESA's Science Programme Committee selected Plasma Observatory at its meeting on 19 November 2026; it fills the medium-class 'M7' slot.

Plasma is the fourth state of matter, an ionised gas of charged particles that responds strongly to electric and magnetic fields; it is uncommon on Earth but makes up more than 99% of visible matter in the Universe, including the Sun and stars.

The Sun constantly releases the solar wind, a stream of plasma; when it meets Earth's magnetic field the strongest interactions produce auroras, and occasionally cause outages in satellites and power grids.

How it works: the seven spacecraft fly in two nested tetrahedral (pyramid-shaped) formations sharing one spacecraft; the inner formation studies small ion-scale processes and the outer one larger fluid-scale behaviour, at the same time.
ESA's earlier Cluster mission found interactions spanning a few kilometres to tens of thousands of kilometres, but could observe only one scale at a time.
ESA asked for M7 proposals in December 2021 and received 27 responses; three finalists were studied before Plasma Observatory was proposed in June 2026.
ESA Director of Science Carole Mundell said the mission 'will enable us to understand how our planet interacts with the sea of plasma around it.'
Study scientist Matt Taylor said: 'We can use Earth's magnetic "bubble" - its magnetosphere - as a natural laboratory.'
Next the mission must be formally 'adopted' before construction begins; no cost has been published.

stories.headline: Rocket that lost 40 Amazon internet satellites was starved of fuel, early findings say
stories.what_happened: On 18 November 2026 United Launch Alliance (ULA) said early evidence shows its Vulcan Centaur rocket failed on 15 November because not enough fuel reached the two BE-4 engines on its first stage. All 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites on board were lost.
stories.why_it_matters: It was Vulcan's first full failure; the rocket is grounded while the investigation continues, which may delay Amazon's plan to build an internet satellite network.

key_facts.fact: ULA said 'preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines', and that the engines themselves were not the cause.
The rocket launched from Florida's Space Coast on 15 November carrying 40 Amazon internet satellites, all of which were lost.

How it works: two BE-4 engines, built by Blue Origin, power Vulcan's first-stage booster; the problem was in the rocket delivering fuel to them, so they could not make enough thrust. ULA said the upper stage worked but could not recover from the booster's lost performance.
ULA said the six solid rocket boosters and the Centaur V upper stage appear to have performed well.
It was Vulcan's fifth flight since its January 2024 debut, and its only failure.
The root cause is still under investigation, overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration; how long Vulcan stays grounded is unknown.

stories.headline: UK and EU agree new deal on youth travel, food trade and carbon markets at Brussels summit
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Andy Burnham met EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November 2026 and agreed a package to bring Britain and the EU closer, ten years after the Brexit vote. It includes a 'Youth Experience Scheme' letting young people live, work or study in each other's countries for up to three years, shared food-standards rules and a link to the EU's electricity carbon market. Days earlier Burnham had said 'The Brexit we were given has not worked.'
stories.why_it_matters: It is the biggest change to UK-EU ties since Britain left the EU in 2020, and the youth scheme directly affects what today's teenagers may be able to do after school.

key_facts.fact: The UK-EU summit took place in Brussels on Friday 20 November 2026, as a key step in Burnham's pledge to reset relations with the 27-member bloc.
The summit came ten years after the 2016 referendum and six years after the UK left the EU in 2020; the 2016 result was 52% leave, 48% remain.
In a speech on 16 November Burnham said: 'The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.' He put the economic damage at 4% to 8% of UK GDP.

Under the new Youth Experience Scheme, about 100,000 young people from EU countries can spend up to three years in Britain travelling, working or studying, with about 100,000 British young people able to go the other way each year.
Burnham said 'Brexit did take away opportunity from young people' and told young Britons 'you will have, as a result of this deal, a new freedom.'
The UK will follow EU food standards rules from March 2028, which ministers say will cut paperwork; Treasury analysis suggests this could add about 0.5% to UK GDP.
The UK will join the EU's electricity carbon emission markets, and the deal includes a commitment to closer defence cooperation.
Further talks on cutting tuition fees for European students at UK universities are still to come.
A bill to put the deal into law is due to be introduced in Parliament the following week.
Oliver Lewis of the Stay Out campaign called it 'a humiliating spectacle for the Prime Minister'.
Until the next general election Burnham is bound by his predecessor Keir Starmer's pledge not to rejoin the EU customs union or single market.
Separately, the EU and UK had already agreed in April 2026 that the UK will rejoin the Erasmus+ student exchange programme in 2027.

stories.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as diesel hits a record price
stories.what_happened: Prices in the UK were 3.6% higher in October 2026 than a year earlier, up from 3.5% in September, the Office for National Statistics said on 18 November. Fuel was the big driver: the average litre of diesel reached 199.5p, the highest since records began in 1996, linked to the conflict in the Middle East pushing up energy prices. Food price rises slowed to their lowest rate since 2021.
stories.why_it_matters: Inflation measures how fast the cost of living is rising; when it stays above the Bank of England's comfort zone, the Bank may raise interest rates, which affects families' mortgages and savings.

key_facts.fact: CPI inflation was 3.6% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 3.5% in September.
Prices rose 0.5% in the single month of October, compared with 0.4% in October 2025.
It was the highest rate since October 2025 and the fourth monthly increase in a row.
Analysts had expected 3.7%, so the figure was slightly lower than forecast.
Motor fuel prices were up 33.2% on a year earlier; diesel rose 7.0p a litre in the month to an average 199.5p, the highest since ONS records began in January 1996.
Petrol rose 5.2p to an average of 174.4p a litre, its highest since August 2022.
Food and non-alcoholic drink inflation eased to 0.9% from 1.3%, the lowest since September 2021.
The rise is linked to the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up global energy prices.
Earlier in November the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to raise Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4%.
The Bank of England's latest Monetary Policy Report said inflation could reach around 5% by the middle of next year.
Core inflation (which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) stayed at 2.8%.

stories.headline: Household energy bills forecast to jump 26% in January
stories.what_happened: Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight predicted on 18 November that the price cap for a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales will rise to about £2,166 a year from January 2027, up 26% from £1,723. It blames high and volatile wholesale gas prices linked to the Middle East conflict. The regulator Ofgem will announce the official figure on 25 November.
stories.why_it_matters: Heating and lighting homes would cost much more in the coldest months, adding to the cost-of-living squeeze shown by rising inflation.

key_facts.fact: Cornwall Insight forecasts the annual price cap for a typical dual-fuel household will reach £2,166 from January 2027, a rise of £443 or 26%.
The current cap is £1,723, after a 4% rise in October; the new level would be the highest since 2023.
The rise is mainly blamed on high, volatile wholesale energy prices, especially gas, linked to disruption from the Middle East conflict.
Ofgem's price cap limits the unit rates and standing charges suppliers can charge, not the total a household pays, and it is reviewed every three months.
The typical household assumed uses 2,500kWh of electricity and 9,500kWh of gas a year; the cap covers England, Scotland and Wales but not Northern Ireland.
Ofgem will announce the official cap on 25 November; the Cornwall Insight figure is only a forecast.
The October budget included a £100 payment for millions of households.

stories.what_happened: An independent review by former minister Alan Milburn, published on 17 November, found 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in England and Wales were not in education, employment or training (NEET). On 18 November the government said it would overhaul support, with locally led youth services from 2027 and a new Youth Opportunities Unit. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wants the report to be 'a watershed moment'.
stories.why_it_matters: It is about the futures of teenagers and young adults - whether there are enough routes into jobs, training and apprenticeships.

key_facts.fact: The review, commissioned by the Work and Pensions Secretary and published by the DWP on 17 November 2026, is called 'From a welfare state to a working state: a new settlement for the next generation'.
981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in England and Wales were NEET between April and June 2026, about 13% of that age group.
It recommends giving young people a legal right to a route into education, training or work, backed by an 'opportunity guarantee'.
It proposes 170,000 extra jobs and apprenticeships through employer incentives, and doubling apprenticeship completions by 2036.
Employers signing up as 'First Chance' employers are asked to work toward filling 10% of entry-level jobs with young people who are NEET or at risk of becoming NEET.
The review warns the number of under-25s affected could reach 1.27 million within five years.
The government plans locally led youth services from 2027 combining employment, health and skills support, shaped by mayors and local leaders, plus a new Youth Opportunities Unit.
Burnham said he wants the report 'to be a watershed moment' for how government and society tackle youth unemployment and inactivity.

stories.headline: Russian missiles land in Poland during one of the war's biggest attacks on Ukraine
stories.what_happened: Overnight into 20 November 2026 Russia fired hundreds of drones and dozens of missiles at Ukraine, damaging three bridges in Kyiv and cutting power, heat and water in places. At least nine people died. Two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone came down inside Poland, an EU and NATO member, without injuring anyone; Poland called it a provocation.
stories.why_it_matters: When Russian weapons land in a NATO country, it raises fears the war could spread, and it came a day after European leaders insisted they must have a say in any peace deal.

key_facts.fact: Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 84 cruise missiles and 404 attack drones; President Zelensky said 27 ballistic missiles were also used.
Air defences shot down or suppressed 3 ballistic missiles, 79 cruise missiles and 380 drones.
Three Kyiv bridges - Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Southern and Darnytskyi - were damaged.
At least nine people were killed, according to Ukraine's prime minister, and the attack disrupted electricity, heating and water supplies.
Putin had vowed revenge for Ukraine's 17 November strike on the Crimean Bridge, saying the response would be 'far more painful'.
A Kh-101 cruise missile landed near the village of Nowy Lipowiec in Lublin province, about 60 km from the Ukrainian border; another missile and a jet-powered drone fell at two other sites.
No injuries or damage to critical infrastructure were reported in Poland.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it a Russian 'provocation' and convened ministers, military and intelligence chiefs.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned the 'grave violations' of Polish airspace and was expected in Warsaw on Saturday.
A Kh-101 missile previously crashed in Tarnawa-Kolonia, eastern Poland, on 30 July.
An energy official said Russia targeted what they called Europe's largest electrical substation.

stories.headline: European leaders meet in Berlin and reject a 'new Yalta' after Trump-Xi-Putin summit
stories.what_happened: While Trump, Xi and Putin met in Shenzhen on 19 November, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted Ukraine's backers - the 'Coalition of the Willing' - in Berlin. Merz called Shenzhen a 'photo op' and said Europe would never again be carved up as at Yalta in 1945. Leaders insisted Europe and Ukraine must be at the table in any peace talks.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows Europe pushing back against big powers deciding Ukraine's and Europe's future without them, and links today's news to a famous moment in history.

key_facts.fact: Merz spoke on Thursday 19 November 2026 after the Coalition of the Willing summit at the Chancellery in Berlin.
Attendees included Zelensky, Macron, von der Leyen, Rutte, Costa, UK PM Andy Burnham and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Merz said: 'At Yalta, Europe was divided up. It was parcelled up. And we won't allow anything like that to happen again.'
The Yalta Conference took place in February 1945 with Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin.
Merz handed participants pieces of the Berlin Wall, saying it brought 'oppression, insecurity and a lack of peace'.
The Shenzhen leaders' four-point 'Declaration toward Peace' covered UN reform, oil supplies, the ICC and nuclear risk, but did not mention Russia's war against Ukraine.
Merz said new peace talks with Europe, Ukraine, Russia and the US could happen soon, naming the UAE as a possible venue.
Poland's Donald Tusk said 'Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be'; Burnham said the US and Europe had reached their first real alignment on Ukraine in months.
Kushner said Russia had agreed to multilateral talks with Europe; Putin proposed European envoys come to Moscow.

Sánchez warned a PP-Vox coalition would roll back social rights; Vox leader Santiago Abascal was not in the debate.

stories.headline: EU creates a Sanctions Office to stop Russia dodging its penalties
stories.what_happened: On 18 November 2026 the European Commission set up a new EU Sanctions Office to design, enforce and stop people getting around its sanctions, and named Swedish diplomat Lars Danielsson as its special sanctions envoy. stories.why_it_matters: Sanctions only work if they cannot be bypassed through other countries or secret routes; this is the EU trying to close the gaps.

key_facts.fact: The office brings together expertise across the 'sanctions lifecycle', from designing measures to enforcement and preventing circumvention, plus outreach to non-EU countries.
It will help EU member states with faster compliance guidance, data sharing and economic analysis so sanctions are applied consistently.
It sits in the Commission's Secretariat-General under Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque; the changes take effect in January 2027.
Lars Danielsson becomes International Special Envoy for the Implementation of EU Sanctions on 6 February 2027, replacing David O'Sullivan.
Circumvention means getting around restrictions through alternative trade routes, financial channels or procurement networks.
